# Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty

Jeonghye Kim Affiliation: Microsoft Research  Affiliation: KAIST   
Xufang Luo ^(†)^(†)thanks: Work done during Jeonghye’s internship at
Microsoft Research. Corresponding author. Our analysis code can be found
at
[link](https://github.com/beanie00/strategic-information-allocation-llm-reasoning).
Affiliation: Microsoft Research     Minbeom Kim Affiliation: Seoul
National University    Sangmook Lee, Dongsheng Li, Yuqing Yang
Affiliation: Microsoft Research  Affiliation: Seoul National University

###### Abstract

LLMs often exhibit Aha moments such as self-correction after tokens like
"Wait," yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. Standard LLMs
collapse mainly through silent divergence, where trajectories drift from
the correct answer yet remain locally coherent, so no explicit error
triggers reactive self-correction. We introduce an information-theoretic
framework that separates reasoning into procedural advancement and
_epistemic verbalization_, the token-level externalization of
uncertainty, and prove that sporadic verbalization restores convergence
toward the correct answer even without explicit error triggers.
Empirically, a minimal doubt cue recovers failed trajectories, and
small-scale SFT suffices to instill or suppress this capability,
suggesting that strong reasoning hinges less on an extraordinary inner
mechanism than on the linguistic habit of externalizing uncertainty. Our
framework recasts reasoning as strategic information allocation under
uncertainty, offering a new lens for understanding and advancing LLM
reasoning.

## 1 Introduction

Recent large language models (LLMs) often exhibit so-called Aha moments
during reasoning, with behaviors such as self-correction or reflection
appearing after tokens like "Wait" ([Guo et al., 2025](#bib.bib5); [Yang
et al., 2025d](#bib.bib4)). These phenomena are frequently cited as key
mechanisms underlying effective reasoning, yet there remains little
consensus on what computational or informational role they actually play
([d’Aliberti and Ribeiro, 2026](#bib.bib18); [Liu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib24); [Tsui, 2025](#bib.bib20)). Prior work tends to group
Aha moments, reflection, self-correction, and the emergence of specific
tokens as a single class of phenomena, making it difficult to
disentangle their underlying mechanisms.

![Refer to caption](2603.15500v2/figure/concept.png)

Figure 1: Two pathways for self-correction. The Procedural channel
reacts only when an explicit violation triggers an alarm, whereas the
Epistemic channel continuously monitors and prompts self-checking even
without any visible contradiction.

In parallel, recent studies have examined reasoning from an
information-theoretic perspective ([Ton et al., 2025](#bib.bib12);
[Liang, 2025](#bib.bib14)), reinterpreting Chain-of-Thought (CoT) ([Wei
et al., 2022b](#bib.bib13)) as a process of information accumulation
toward the correct answer. While offering valuable insights, these
approaches largely assume procedural, step-by-step execution and do not
fully account for the self-corrective behaviors of modern reasoning
models, particularly recovery after entering an incorrect trajectory.
Once execution enters an erroneous path, reasoning may remain locally
coherent yet globally incorrect, with the underlying error unrecognized.

To investigate this gap, we analyze the reasoning behavior of standard
LLMs and large reasoning models (LRMs). LLMs rely almost exclusively on
_reactive correction_, revising their trajectory only when an explicit
contradiction or failed check surfaces. When errors remain latent, no
trigger arises and the trace drifts into reasoning collapse, the
dominant failure mode. LRMs additionally exhibit _proactive correction_,
questioning prior steps without any overt error and surfacing hidden
mistakes that reactive mechanisms cannot reach (Figure
[1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")).
Although such proactive signals are imprecise and often second-guess
already-correct chains, in this regime even a noisy signal is more
useful than a precise one that never fires.

Building on this observation, we identify an additional informational
axis distinct from procedural information. Our key idea is _epistemic
uncertainty verbalization_, the explicit externalization at the token
level of a model’s internal uncertainty about its reasoning state. Since
autoregressive generation conditions only on preceding tokens, latent
uncertainty is informationally inert, whereas verbalized uncertainty
becomes actionable and supports downstream control actions such as
self-correction. From this perspective, commonly discussed tokens such
as "Wait" are surface manifestations of epistemic verbalization rather
than the mechanism itself, and reasoning can be reframed as _strategic
information allocation under uncertainty_: the joint determination of
how to advance the procedure and how much epistemic verbalization to
allocate at each step, given the model’s current uncertainty.

We empirically validate that epistemic verbalization carries substantive
information for reasoning. On failed trajectories, injecting a minimal
doubt cue such as "Wait, is that correct?", without identifying what
went wrong, recovers around 15% of incorrect rollouts, showing that the
externalization of uncertainty itself supplies actionable signal. We
further show that epistemic verbalization is a rapidly learnable
capability. In line with the findings of [Ye et al. (2025)](#bib.bib1),
as few as 800 training samples suffice to either instill or suppress
this behavior, indicating that externalizing internal uncertainty
requires no extraordinary ability but rather reflects a linguistic
habit. Our new taxonomy and framing of LLM reasoning offers a unified
lens for interpreting Aha moments, self-correction, and post-training
phenomena, and points toward principled directions for designing and
controlling reasoning models.

## 2 Related Works

#### Understanding Aha moments.

Recent studies have cast doubt on Aha-like phenomena in LLM reasoning.
[d’Aliberti and Ribeiro (2026)](#bib.bib18) show that markers such as
“Wait” emerge from high-entropy prediction states and correlate only
weakly with performance gains. [Liu et al. (2025)](#bib.bib24) find that
apparent self-reflection often degenerates into repetition rather than
producing constructive revisions. A related line of evidence shows that
LLMs correct externally provided errors yet fail to fix the same errors
in their own outputs ([Tsui, 2025](#bib.bib20); [Huang et al.,
2024](#bib.bib21); [Tyen et al., 2024](#bib.bib22); [Kamoi et al.,
2024](#bib.bib23)). These studies document when Aha tokens fail to
predict correction, but leave open why: the marker itself may be
unreliable, the model may lack a corrective policy, or both. The
underlying mechanism remains unidentified.

#### Theoretical understanding of reasoning.

A parallel line of work analyzes reasoning trajectories at the aggregate
level. [Yang et al. (2025c)](#bib.bib15) show that reasoning can both
fix and introduce errors by decoupling knowledge-based responses from
reasoning-based corrections. [Gan et al. (2025)](#bib.bib16) recast CoT
as optimization over reasoning states and identify trade-offs between
noise reduction and generalization. Information-theoretic analyses show
that CoT preserves task-relevant information and tightens error bounds
([Ton et al., 2025](#bib.bib12); [Liang, 2025](#bib.bib14)). [Qian et
al. (2025)](#bib.bib19) observe that effective reasoning concentrates
information gain in a few critical steps, often marked by tokens like
“Wait.” These accounts describe how information flows across a
trajectory but treat every token as a procedural step, leaving
unexplained how a model recovers after drifting onto an incorrect path
without outside help.

We close both gaps with a unified information-theoretic framework of
reasoning at the token level. First, we identify _epistemic
verbalization_, the externalization of uncertainty about one’s own
reasoning, as the informational source that lets a model regain traction
after a procedural misstep, and prove that even sporadic occurrences
suffice to restore convergence. Second, we separate this informational
role from the _control actions_, such as self-correction, that act on
it. Together, these results reconcile the mixed empirical findings on
Aha moments and supply the token-level grounding missing from aggregate
information-theoretic accounts.

## 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning

Our analysis mainly focuses on the _closed-world inference setting_,
where an LLM operates without external observations at inference time.
Unlike tool-augmented agents that reduce uncertainty through
environmental interaction, a closed-world LLM is constrained to a fixed
parameterization $`\theta`$ and an initial input $`x`$, so all progress
toward correct inference must come from internal belief transformation.
We formalize this as self-Bayesian reasoning, where CoT ([Wei et al.,
2022a](#bib.bib10)) acts as _self-conditioning_ that reshapes the
model’s belief over the target variable $`Y`$ without new external
observations.
Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B World-Bayesian Reasoning with External Observations ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
extends this to the open-world setting.

### 3.1 Reasoning as Self-Conditioning

Given an input $`x\in\mathcal{X}`$, an LLM parameterized by $`\theta`$
induces a conditional distribution $`P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x)`$ over
tokens from vocabulary $`\mathcal{V}`$, and autoregressively generates a
sequence $`a_{1},\dots,a_{T}`$ until terminal step $`T`$. We define the
reasoning state at step $`t`$ as

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
s_{0}:=x,\qquad s_{t}:=(x,a_{1},\dots,a_{t})\text{ for }t\geq 1,
``` |  | (1) |

so that each token is drawn as
$`a_{t}\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t-1})`$. Each state $`s_{t}`$
induces a predictive distribution $`P_{\theta}(Y\mid s_{t})`$ over the
target variable $`Y\in\mathcal{Y}`$, and we take the objective of
reasoning to be the minimization of $`H(Y\mid s_{T})`$, where
$`H(\cdot)`$ denotes Shannon entropy. Reasoning thus proceeds by
*self-conditioning*: each generated token refines the model’s belief
over $`Y`$ without introducing external evidence, and the information
gain of a step is

|     |                                              |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \Delta_{t}:=H(Y\mid s_{t-1})-H(Y\mid s_{t}).
       ```                                           |     | (2) |

Self-generated intermediate steps serve as the model’s sole source of
evidence, making their informational quality critical for reasoning
success.

### 3.2 Procedural Reasoning and Its Collapse

A dominant class of self-generated evidence in LLM reasoning consists of
procedural information: explicit step-by-step computations, symbolic
manipulations, variable instantiations, and executions of learned
subroutines ([Lai et al., 2024](#bib.bib8); [Feng et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9); [Oh et al., 2025](#bib.bib30); [Ton et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12)). Formally, let $`0=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdots<t_{K}=T`$
partition a reasoning trace into sub-tasks with task-level state
$`U_{k}:=(x,a_{1},\dots,a_{t_{k}})`$. Procedural reasoning is then a
sequence $`U_{k}=\Lambda_{\theta}(U_{k-1},\tau_{k})`$, where
$`\Lambda_{\theta}`$ is an autoregressive execution operator
implementing sub-task $`\tau_{k}`$.

#### Reasoning collapse in standard LLMs.

We examine how this regime fails in practice by analyzing reasoning
traces from the Qwen2.5 and Qwen3-Base series (Qwen2.5-7B,
Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct, Qwen2.5-Math-7B ([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib7)),
Qwen3-1.7B/8B/14B-Base ([Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib6))) on AIME24/25,
AMC23, and MATH500. These models exhibit strong step-by-step procedural
reasoning ability, achieve competitive performance on these benchmarks,
and serve as standard baselines in recent math reasoning research ([Ye
et al., 2025](#bib.bib1); [Li et al., 2025](#bib.bib2); [Wang et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3); [Yang et al., 2025d](#bib.bib4)). Using GPT-5 as an
automated judge on 4,800 generated samples (600 problems × 8 samples),
we quantify the prevalence of five recurring modes of reasoning collapse
across the traces
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Reasoning collapse in standard LLMs. ‣ 3.2 Procedural Reasoning and Its Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")):
incoherence, hallucination spirals, repetition, topic drift, and
degenerate loops. Collapse is pervasive, occurring in 50–83% of
incorrect responses and rising sharply with problem difficulty
(Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Reasoning collapse in standard LLMs. ‣ 3.2 Procedural Reasoning and Its Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")a).
See
Appendix [D.1](#A4.SS1 "D.1 Reasoning Collapse Analysis ‣ Appendix D Details of the Analysis ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
for details.

![Refer to caption](2603.15500v2/reasoning_collapse_summary.png)

Figure 2: Reasoning collapse analysis across models and benchmarks. (a)
Collapse rate among incorrect responses per model and dataset. (b)
Breakdown of collapse types per model. Model names omit the “Qwen”
prefix (e.g., 2.5-7B refers to Qwen2.5-7B).

In each mode, the surface structure of step-by-step execution is
preserved while $`P_{\theta}(Y\mid s_{t})`$ drifts from the correct
$`Y`$, often without overt error. This silent divergence is the dominant
failure pattern, consistent with prior observations that procedural
reasoning is brittle when a sub-task is *unidentifiable* ([Ton et al.,
2025](#bib.bib12)) or silently misinstantiated through an early
misjudgment.

### 3.3 How Models Escape (or Fail to Escape) Collapse

We next ask how models escape, or fail to escape, these regimes. For
each self-correction event in the traces above, together with traces
from Large Reasoning Models (LRMs: DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/32B ([Guo
et al., 2025](#bib.bib5)), Qwen3-8B/14B ([Yang et al.,
2025a](#bib.bib6))), we distinguish two modes:

- •
  Reactive correction. The reasoning chain contains an explicit error,
  such as a contradiction, a failed check, or an invalid derivation,
  that the model recognizes and revises.
- •
  Proactive correction. No overt error has surfaced, yet the model
  questions a prior step and verifies or backtracks on internal doubt
  alone.

|      |                          |            |            |
|------|--------------------------|------------|------------|
| Type | Model                    | Reactive   | Proactive  |
|      |                          | $`n`$ (%)  | $`n`$ (%)  |
| LLM  | Qwen3-1.7B-Base^(†)      | 12 (100.0) | 0 (0.0)    |
|      | Qwen3-8B-Base^(†)        | 19 (86.4)  | 3 (13.6)   |
|      | Qwen3-14B-Base^(†)       | 23 (92.0)  | 2 (8.0)    |
|      | Qwen2.5-7B^(†)           | 11 (100.0) | 0 (0.0)    |
|      | Qwen2.5-Math-7B^(†)      | 35 (79.5)  | 9 (20.5)   |
|      | Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct^(†) | 8 (80.0)   | 2 (20.0)   |
| LRM  | Qwen3-8B                 | 576 (76.3) | 179 (23.7) |
|      | Qwen3-14B                | 484 (77.8) | 138 (22.2) |
|      | DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B   | 475 (65.0) | 256 (35.0) |
|      | DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B  | 471 (69.3) | 209 (30.7) |

For each generation, a GPT-5-based filter flags traces with a *wrong
path $`\rightarrow`$ correction $`\rightarrow`$ correct answer* pattern;
$`n`$ is the number of such traces per model. Proactive correction is
largely absent in LLMs and emerges consistently in LRMs. ^(†)Small

Examples of both types of modes are provided in
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Examples of Reactive and Proactive Correction ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty").
In LLMs, self-correction occurs in at most 35 of 4,800 generations
(under 1%) and is overwhelmingly reactive
(Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 How Models Escape (or Fail to Escape) Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")).
Reactive correction is the dominant escape mechanism, but it only works
when errors surface as overt local mistakes. The collapse modes of
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Reasoning collapse in standard LLMs. ‣ 3.2 Procedural Reasoning and Its Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
produce no such signal, so reactive correction has nothing to trigger
on, and the trace silently diverges, ultimately leading to collapse.

### 3.4 Proactive Correction in LRMs

LRMs exhibit a markedly different pattern. As shown in
Table [1](#S3.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 3.3 How Models Escape (or Fail to Escape) Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
proactive corrections account for 22–35% of all self-corrections. These
corrections arise without any overt error: the model pauses, questions a
prior step, and either verifies or backtracks based on internal doubt
alone, as shown in
Appendix [I](#A9 "Appendix I Examples of Reactive and Proactive Correction ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty").
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Proactive Correction in LRMs ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
situates this capability in the broader model landscape. Standard LLMs
cluster along the bottom of the plot regardless of their direct fluency,
whereas reasoning-tuned models occupy a distinct upper-right region
where higher direct fluency is paired with a qualitatively new capacity
for proactive correction.

Figure 3: Capability map across model families. The $`x`$-axis reports
*direct fluency*, the share of responses answered correctly without
invoking any self-correction, computed as
$`(\text{correct}-\text{SC})/N`$. The $`y`$-axis reports the *proactive
correction rate*, the share of responses containing a suspicion-based
self-correction, i.e., a correction triggered without explicit evidence
of error.

#### Precision of proactive signals.

Since proactive correction is preventive, the model may flag and
re-check something that turns out to be fine. In other words, prevalence
does not imply accuracy.
Table [2](#S3.T2 "Table 2 ‣ Precision of proactive signals. ‣ 3.4 Proactive Correction in LRMs ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
reports the *precision* of proactive signals, defined as the fraction of
suspicion-triggered corrections issued on a trajectory that was in fact
wrong. Across LRMs, precision averages only $`24.4\%`$: roughly three
out of four proactive verbalizations second-guess an already-correct
chain. DeepSeek-R1 distillations are better calibrated ($`37.3\%`$,
$`23.9\%`$) than the Qwen3 series ($`20.5\%`$, $`15.8\%`$), and
precision does not improve with scale.

|                                |                 |
|--------------------------------|-----------------|
|  Model                         |  Precision (%)  |
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B   |  37.3           |
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B  |  23.9           |
|  Qwen3-8B                      |  20.5           |
|  Qwen3-14B                     |  15.8           |

Table 2: Precision of proactive self-correction signals across LRMs.
Precision is the fraction of suspicion-based corrections issued on
genuinely incorrect trajectories, as judged by GPT-5 (See Appendix
[D.2](#A4.SS2 "D.2 Reactive and Proactive Correction Analysis ‣ Appendix D Details of the Analysis ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
for details). The remainder second-guess already-correct chains.

However, low precision does not undermine the role of proactive
correction. The silent divergences in
Figure [2](#S3.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ Reasoning collapse in standard LLMs. ‣ 3.2 Procedural Reasoning and Its Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
never produce an overt error, so reactive correction has no trigger to
act on. In this regime, even a noisy extra signal is more useful than a
precise reactive one that never fires. Proactive correction is what
brings these hidden errors to the surface and lets the model recover,
allowing strong reasoners to maintain trajectory quality where reactive
correction cannot reach. We now term this mechanism *epistemic
verbalization*.

## 4 Epistemic Verbalization

#### Definition.

Epistemic verbalization is the linguistic channel through which the
model explicitly externalizes uncertainty about its own trajectory,
turning otherwise inert internal assessments into conditionable tokens
that subsequent reasoning can act on. Reasoning traces of strong models
contain utterances that do not advance procedural execution but instead
express judgments of uncertainty or doubt about intermediate steps
(Table [3](#S4.T3 "Table 3 ‣ Definition. ‣ 4 Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")).

|  |  |
|----|----|
| \# |  Example |
| 1 |  Wait, is that correct? |
| 2 |  Wait, 2023 is 7 multiplied by 17 squared, right? |
| 3 |  Wait, maybe $`f(n)`$ is related to the Möbius function but scaled differently. |
| 4 |  Wait, perhaps I can write it as $`(f*(n/d))(n)=1`$, but that doesn’t seem helpful. |

Table 3: Examples of epistemic verbalizations co-occurring with “Wait”
in reasoning traces from DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B/7B/32B.

Let $`Z_{t}`$ denote a latent epistemic variable at step $`t`$,
representing the model’s internal assessment of its trajectory’s
reliability. As a latent quantity, $`Z_{t}`$ is informationally inert:
although $`I(Y;Z_{t}\mid s_{t-1})`$ may be strictly positive, this
information remains trapped inside the model’s internal states. Since
autoregressive decoding conditions on the realized token sequence
$`s_{t-1}`$, not on internal states, $`Z_{t}`$ cannot influence
subsequent generation. Epistemic verbalization closes this gap by
emitting tokens $`v_{t}`$ from which $`Z_{t}`$ is recoverable. Once
$`v_{t}\in s_{t}`$, we have

|     |                                              |     |     |
|-----|----------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       H(Y\mid s_{t-1},v_{t})\leq H(Y\mid s_{t-1}),
       ```                                           |     | (3) |

with strict inequality whenever $`v_{t}`$ carries non-trivial
information about $`Z_{t}`$. Epistemic verbalization is thus the
mechanism by which latent assessments become causally active in
reasoning.

### 4.1 Injecting Epistemic Verbalization Recovers Failed Trajectories.

We empirically validate that epistemic verbalization supplies actionable
information beyond procedural reasoning through an intervention study on
failed reasoning trajectories.

We collect all incorrect rollouts from Qwen3-8B/14B-Base, which
predominantly exhibit procedural reasoning
(Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Procedural Reasoning and Its Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")),
on three benchmarks (AIME24, AMC23, MATH500) with 8 rollouts per
problem. Since every rollout is incorrect, it must diverge from a valid
path at some unknown point. We therefore sweep candidate truncation
points: for each rollout, we truncate at relative position
$`\alpha\in\{0.2,0.5,0.8,0.9\}`$ and resume generation from that point,
optionally inserting a short epistemic verbalization.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Condition |  Phrase |
|  None |  (no injection) |
|  Hmm-Doubt |  “Hmm, I’m not sure this is right.” |
|  Hmm-Doubt-Revisit |  “Hmm, I’m not sure this is right. Let me reconsider.” |
|  Wait-Doubt |  “Wait, is that correct?” |
|  Wait-Revisit |  “Wait, let me double-check.” |

Table 4: Injection conditions. Four epistemic phrases span two phrase
types (Hmm, Wait) and vary in whether they express doubt alone, signal
an intent to revisit, or both. None controls for the effect of mere
re-sampling from the truncated prefix.

We compare five conditions
(Table [4](#S4.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 4.1 Injecting Epistemic Verbalization Recovers Failed Trajectories. ‣ 4 Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")).
The None baseline performs no injection. The other four are epistemic
phrases that vary along two axes. The first axis is phrase type (Hmm vs.
Wait), and the second is function. Doubt expresses uncertainty alone,
Revisit signals an intent to re-examine the reasoning, and Doubt-Revisit
combines the two. Because it is unknown whether the truncation point
occurs before or after the divergence point, the None condition isolates
the effect of re-sampling alone. For each condition we draw $`n=4`$
continuations and report the *recovery rate*: the fraction of originally
incorrect rollouts whose continuation reaches the correct answer.

Figure 4: Recovery rate vs. truncation fraction $`\alpha`$ across
injection conditions and benchmarks, for Qwen3-8B-Base (top) and
Qwen3-14B-Base (bottom).

Figure [4](#S4.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ 4.1 Injecting Epistemic Verbalization Recovers Failed Trajectories. ‣ 4 Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
reports recovery rates across conditions, truncation positions, and
benchmarks. Across all settings, simply expressing uncertainty, without
pinpointing what went wrong, acts as an informative signal that drives
recovery. Notably, even Doubt, which conveys only uncertainty without
any explicit cue to re-examine the reasoning (e.g., "Hmm, I’m not sure
…"), suffices for the model to detect its own errors and recover the
correct answer. Recovery rates decline as $`\alpha`$ increases, but the
baseline decays fastest, dropping to near zero at $`\alpha=0.9`$, so the
gap between injected cues and the baseline widens with $`\alpha`$.
Differences among phrasings are small, though "Wait"-style cues slightly
outperform "Hmm"-style ones. Overall recovery tracks benchmark
difficulty (MATH500 $`>`$ AMC23 $`>`$ AIME24), and the same pattern
holds for both Qwen3-8B-Base and Qwen3-14B-Base, indicating robustness
to model scale.

### 4.2 Epistemic Tokens as Measurement Proxies

The linguistic realizations of uncertainty expression can be numerous
and diverse, making full semantic analysis infeasible at scale. Still,
surface tokens provide a useful observational handle on where
verbalization is likely occurring.

To identify which surface tokens reliably co-occur with epistemic
verbalization, we analyzed reasoning traces from four models
(Qwen3-8/14B and DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B/32B) on math benchmarks and
measured how frequently each candidate token appeared using GPT-5 as a
judge. Details are provided in
Appendix [D.4](#A4.SS4 "D.4 Identifying Epistemic Tokens ‣ Appendix D Details of the Analysis ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty").
The resulting frequencies were: "wait" (73.0%), "maybe" (32.9%),
"actually" (12.4%), "check" (10.5%), "hmm" (8.3%), "perhaps" (8.2%),
"might" (6.6%), "seems" (3.3%), and "alternatively" (1.2%).

We therefore adopt these nine terms as epistemic tokens: "wait", "hmm",
"perhaps", "maybe", "actually", "alternatively", "seems", "might", and
"check" as practical indicators of regions where epistemic verbalization
likely occurs.

## 5 A Unified Framework: Reasoning as Strategic Information Allocation

We now formalize the analysis of Sections
[3](#S3 "3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")–[4](#S4 "4 Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
within a unified information-theoretic framework: reasoning under
uncertainty operates along two informational axes, procedural
advancement and epistemic verbalization, on which control actions such
as self-correction subsequently act.

### 5.1 Epistemic Verbalization Enables Continued Information Acquisition

Procedural reasoning operates by proceeding along the correct path or
revising an incorrect one when explicit errors are detected. Epistemic
verbalization, by contrast, exposes information about the reliability of
the current trajectory regardless of whether any error has surfaced,
thereby altering the model’s effective belief state. We formalize this
distinction by specifying when procedural reasoning alone becomes
insufficient and showing that even sporadic epistemic verbalization
suffices to restore convergence.

###### Assumption 5.1 (Procedural Information is Trigger-Conditional).

Suppose the procedural trajectory enters a diverged execution path at
sub-task index $`k^{*}`$. For $`k>k^{*}`$, let $`E_{k}\in\{0,1\}`$
indicate whether sub-task $`\tau_{k}`$ surfaces an overt error available
to procedural revision, and let
$`p_{E}:=\mathbb{P}(E_{k}=1\mid U_{k-1})`$. There exists
$`\delta_{\mathrm{proc}}>0`$ such that

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
I(Y;U_{k}\mid U_{k-1})\;\geq\;\delta_{\mathrm{proc}}\quad\text{only if }E_{k}=1.
``` |  |

Procedural information about $`Y`$ thus accumulates only when overt
errors surface along the diverged path. In the silent-divergence regime
characterized in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Procedural Reasoning and Its Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
the surface structure of step-by-step execution is preserved even as
$`P_{\theta}(Y\mid U_{k})`$ drifts from the correct $`Y`$, so
$`p_{E}\approx 0`$ and procedural information acquisition stalls in
expectation.

###### Assumption 5.2 (Epistemic Informativeness).

There exist $`\delta>0`$ and a threshold $`\eta>0`$ such that, at every
step $`t`$ where an epistemic token is generated with
$`H(Y\mid\tilde{S}_{t-1})>\eta`$,

|     |                                                              |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       H(Y\mid\tilde{S}_{t-1})-H(Y\mid\tilde{S}_{t})\;\geq\;\delta,
       ```                                                           |     |

independently of whether an overt error has surfaced at the current
sub-task.

Intuitively, whenever uncertainty about $`Y`$ is still substantial,
generating an epistemic token yields a non-trivial reduction in that
uncertainty, regardless of whether the procedural channel has flagged an
error. The key property is thus *trigger-independence*: epistemic
verbalization can introduce information gain even when $`p_{E}\to 0`$.
This is consistent with the intervention study in
Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Injecting Epistemic Verbalization Recovers Failed Trajectories. ‣ 4 Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
where injecting a doubt cue alone, without pinpointing any error,
meaningfully enabled the recovery of failed trajectories. In addition,
we empirically demonstrate in
Appendix [F](#A6 "Appendix F Epistemic Verbalization Produces Information Gain ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
that epistemic verbalization introduces information by analyzing the
mutual information between epistemic verbalization and $`Y`$.

###### Proposition 5.3 (Sporadic Epistemic Verbalization Suffices for Convergence).

Under
Assumption [5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Assumption 5.2 (Epistemic Informativeness). ‣ 5.1 Epistemic Verbalization Enables Continued Information Acquisition ‣ 5 A Unified Framework: Reasoning as Strategic Information Allocation ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
if an epistemic token is generated with at least some non-zero
probability $`\rho`$ whenever $`H(Y\mid\tilde{S}_{t})>\eta`$, then
$`\mathbb{E}[H(Y\mid\tilde{S}_{t})]\to 0`$ as $`t\to\infty`$, regardless
of the procedural trigger probability $`p_{E}`$.

The formal statement and proof are deferred to
Appendix [A](#A1 "Appendix A Proof of Proposition ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty").
This explains the empirical pattern in
Section [3](#S3 "3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty").
LLMs rely on reactive correction and thus fail in silent-divergence
regimes where no procedural trigger arises, whereas LRMs sustain a
non-trivial rate of epistemic verbalization that keeps belief
contracting in the same regimes.

### 5.2 Self-Correction as a Control Action

Building on the distinction between procedural and epistemic
information, we now separate *information* from *control*.
Self-correction is a control action that fires whenever an error
surfaces in the reasoning chain. Epistemic verbalization does not itself
perform correction. It is a conditionable informational mechanism that
renders the model’s uncertainty at the token level, enabling the policy
to control the reasoning trajectory accordingly.

Taken together, these results characterize reasoning as *strategic
information allocation under uncertainty*: a process in which an LLM
balances procedural and epistemic information acquisition and then
performs appropriate control actions based on that information.

## 6 Experiments

### 6.1 Test-Time Control of Epistemic Tokens

Following the previous finding that injecting epistemic verbalization
meaningfully recovers failed trajectories
(Section [4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Injecting Epistemic Verbalization Recovers Failed Trajectories. ‣ 4 Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")),
we conversely manipulate the epistemic tokens defined in
Section [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Epistemic Tokens as Measurement Proxies ‣ 4 Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
at test time to further analyze their impact on reasoning performance.
Specifically, we use DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B/32B ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5)) and compare standard inference against inference in
which epistemic tokens are suppressed.

Figure 5: Comparison of avg@8 between baseline inference and inference
with epistemic tokens suppressed on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-14B/32B.

As shown in
Figure [5](#S6.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 6.1 Test-Time Control of Epistemic Tokens ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
masking epistemic tokens results in performance drops around 10%. While
suppression substantially disrupts uncertainty expression, performance
does not collapse entirely. Analysis of the reasoning traces
(Appendix [H.1](#A8.SS1 "H.1 Bypass Pathways under Epistemic Token Suppression ‣ Appendix H Quantitative Analysis ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"))
shows that the models sometimes route around the masked tokens by
adopting alternative forms of epistemic verbalization.

### 6.2 Suppressing Epistemic Verbalization via Distillation

To rule out such circumvention and isolate the effect of epistemic
verbalization more cleanly, we design a controlled self-distillation SFT
experiment. For each base model, we fine-tune it on 800 of its own
reasoning traces generated with epistemic verbalization suppressed.
Specifically, we append the instruction *"Proceed directly without
expressing uncertainty or doubt within the reasoning steps."* to the
prompt, collect 800 problems the model answers correctly under this
prompt, and use the resulting traces as SFT data. This yields a
fine-tuned variant whose training traces differ from the base model’s
natural reasoning only in the absence of epistemic verbalization.

|                           |        |               |
|---------------------------|--------|---------------|
|                           |  Base  |  SFT (no EV)  |
|  Qwen2.5-7B               |  13.3  |  6.7          |
|  Qwen3-8B-Base            |  16.7  |  3.3          |
|  Qwen3-14B-Base           |  16.7  |  10.0         |
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-7B   |  50.0  |  30.0         |
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B  |  80.0  |  43.3         |

Table 5: AIME24 pass@1 across base models and SFT variants trained on
traces with epistemic verbalization (EV) suppressed.

As shown in
Table [5](#S6.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 6.2 Suppressing Epistemic Verbalization via Distillation ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
training on traces with epistemic verbalization suppressed consistently
degrades performance, cutting accuracy by more than half in some cases
despite the fact that all training traces contain correct answers. To
better understand this degradation, we revisit the per-model capability
map in
Figure [3](#S3.F3 "Figure 3 ‣ 3.4 Proactive Correction in LRMs ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
that plots direct fluency against proactive correction rate. There, LRMs
exhibit direct fluency comparable to that of LLMs but substantially
higher proactive correction rates. Interestingly, suppressing epistemic
verbalization through fine-tuning lowers their proactive correction
rate, projecting the LRMs onto the LLM region of the map and bringing
both their reasoning performance and behavior in line with those of
LLMs. This further indicates that epistemic verbalization is not mere
verbosity or stylistic decoration, but a substantive axis of reasoning
capability.

### 6.3 Impact of Epistemic Verbalization on Reasoning Distillation

We further examine the effects of distillation on a public dataset rich
in epistemic verbalizations across several models, and find that
epistemic verbalization is rapidly distilled and translates into quick
performance gains when certain conditions are met, where the degree of
distributional alignment on epistemic tokens plays a critical role. We
use the LIMO-v2 dataset ([Ye et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)), which was
gathered from DeepSeek R1, DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B ([Guo et al.,
2025](#bib.bib5)), and QwQ-32B ([Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib6)), and,
as shown in
Figure [6](#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.3 Impact of Epistemic Verbalization on Reasoning Distillation ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
contains a substantial number of epistemic tokens. Like our SFT setup in
Section [6.2](#S6.SS2 "6.2 Suppressing Epistemic Verbalization via Distillation ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
LIMO consists of only 800 examples, making it far too small to instill
mathematical knowledge and instead serving primarily to reshape the
model’s linguistic habits.

Figure 6: Per-sample epistemic token counts in LIMO. "Wait" alone
appears 77 times per response on average.

Figure [7](#S6.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 6.3 Impact of Epistemic Verbalization on Reasoning Distillation ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
shows the AIME24 pass@1 scores of various models trained on the same
LIMO dataset. For Qwen2.5-7B and Qwen3-8B/14B-Base, performance rapidly
improves by up to 2.6x with only 800 samples, indicating that epistemic
verbalization is not a special model capability but rather a linguistic
habit that is easily distilled. In contrast, other models exhibit
substantial performance degradation despite being trained on the same
dataset with similar initial accuracy and model size.

Figure 7: Comparison of AIME24 pass@1 scores between base models and
models trained with SFT on the LIMO-v2 dataset.

To explain this discrepancy, we analyze distributional alignment between
the student models and the dataset via token-level log probabilities,
focusing on how students evaluate frequent epistemic tokens such as
"Wait" and "Alternatively." The contrast between successful and failed
distillation is clear: as shown in
Figure [8](#S6.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 6.3 Impact of Epistemic Verbalization on Reasoning Distillation ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
successful models exhibit well-aligned distributions in which epistemic
tokens fall within the model’s support, whereas poorly performing models
show large gaps that place these tokens outside the support, hindering
the adoption of the dataset’s epistemic verbalization and control.
Notably, in well-performing models, epistemic tokens remain
low-probability and high-entropy relative to other tokens.

Together, the dispersion in distillation effectiveness from a
high-reasoning model can be attributed to whether the base model’s
pre-existing characteristics are sufficiently "warmed up" to follow the
high-reasoning model’s epistemic verbalization. When the base model can
readily absorb this ability, performance improves rapidly with only a
small dataset, regardless of model size.

![Refer to caption](2603.15500v2/figure/wait_vs_overall_comparison.png)

Figure 8: Distributions of token-level log-probability and entropy for
all tokens versus the subset of "Wait" and "Alternative" tokens.
Vertical blue and red lines indicate the dataset-level averages for
"Wait" and "Alternative" tokens, respectively.

## 7 Conclusion

In this work, we study effective reasoning in LLMs from an
information-theoretic perspective, foregrounding the role of epistemic
verbalization under uncertainty. We show that externalizing uncertainty
enables continued information acquisition and self-correction, and
reframe reasoning as a strategic allocation of information between
procedural and epistemic axes. Empirically, we demonstrate that a
minimal doubt cue suffices to recover failed trajectories, and that as
few as 800 training samples can instill or suppress epistemic
verbalization, suggesting it functions as a learnable linguistic habit
rather than an intrinsic model capability. By distinguishing these two
axes and their associated control actions, our framework clarifies
otherwise elusive phenomena such as Aha moments and provides a general
lens on contemporary LLM reasoning. We hope this perspective informs
future theoretical work and inspires new approaches to modeling and
controlling reasoning under uncertainty.

## Limitations

Our empirical analysis is mainly conducted on mathematical reasoning
benchmarks, where correctness is objectively verifiable. Extending the
analysis to other closed-world reasoning tasks and developing the formal
world-Bayesian extension
(Appendix [B](#A2 "Appendix B World-Bayesian Reasoning with External Observations ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"))
for open-world settings such as tool-augmented or interactive agents are
left for future work. As discussed in Appendix
[B](#A2 "Appendix B World-Bayesian Reasoning with External Observations ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
external observations in such settings can independently surface latent
errors, potentially reducing the model’s reliance on epistemic
verbalization. Empirically characterizing this trade-off is an
interesting direction for future investigation.

Moreover, the nine epistemic tokens in
Sections [4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 Epistemic Tokens as Measurement Proxies ‣ 4 Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
and [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Test-Time Control of Epistemic Tokens ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
serve as practical proxies and do not cover the full range of
uncertainty expressions. While our core results do not rely on this
specific set, a more thorough linguistic analysis of these proxies may
be warranted. Finally, the classification of reactive and proactive
correction, as well as the reasoning collapse analysis, depends on GPT-5
as an automated judge, introducing potential annotation noise.

## Appendix A Proof of Proposition [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition 5.3 (Sporadic Epistemic Verbalization Suffices for Convergence). ‣ 5.1 Epistemic Verbalization Enables Continued Information Acquisition ‣ 5 A Unified Framework: Reasoning as Strategic Information Allocation ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")

We first restate
Proposition [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition 5.3 (Sporadic Epistemic Verbalization Suffices for Convergence). ‣ 5.1 Epistemic Verbalization Enables Continued Information Acquisition ‣ 5 A Unified Framework: Reasoning as Strategic Information Allocation ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
in a formal form that makes the dependence on $`(\rho,\delta,\eta)`$
explicit, and then provide a proof.

###### Proposition A.1.

Let $`H_{t}:=H(Y\mid\tilde{S}_{t})`$ and
$`\tau_{\eta}:=\inf\{t\geq 0:H_{t}\leq\eta\}`$. Suppose
Assumption [5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Assumption 5.2 (Epistemic Informativeness). ‣ 5.1 Epistemic Verbalization Enables Continued Information Acquisition ‣ 5 A Unified Framework: Reasoning as Strategic Information Allocation ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
holds, and that at every step $`t`$ with $`H_{t-1}>\eta`$, an epistemic
token is generated with probability at least $`\rho\in(0,1]`$
(conditional on $`\tilde{S}_{t-1}`$). Then

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\tau_{\eta}]\;\leq\;\frac{\mathbb{E}[H_{0}]-\eta}{\rho\,\delta},
``` |  |

*regardless of the procedural trigger probability $`p_{E}`$*. If such
pairs $`(\rho(\eta),\delta(\eta))`$ exist for every $`\eta>0`$, then
$`\mathbb{E}[H_{t}]\to 0`$ as $`t\to\infty`$.

###### Proof.

Let $`V_{t}\in\{0,1\}`$ indicate whether an epistemic token is generated
at step $`t`$, and let $`\Delta_{t}:=H_{t-1}-H_{t}\geq 0`$. By
Assumption [5.2](#S5.Thmtheorem2 "Assumption 5.2 (Epistemic Informativeness). ‣ 5.1 Epistemic Verbalization Enables Continued Information Acquisition ‣ 5 A Unified Framework: Reasoning as Strategic Information Allocation ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
and the lower bound $`\mathbb{P}(V_{t}=1\mid\tilde{S}_{t-1})\geq\rho`$,
on the event $`\{H_{t-1}>\eta\}`$ we have

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[\Delta_{t}\mid\tilde{S}_{t-1}]\;\geq\;\delta\cdot\mathbb{P}(V_{t}=1\mid\tilde{S}_{t-1})\;\geq\;\rho\,\delta,
``` |  |

which depends only on $`(\rho,\delta)`$ and not on $`p_{E}`$.
Telescoping up to $`\tau_{\eta}`$ and taking expectations,

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
\mathbb{E}[H_{0}]-\eta\;\geq\;\mathbb{E}[H_{0}]-\mathbb{E}[H_{\tau_{\eta}}]\;\geq\;\rho\,\delta\cdot\mathbb{E}[\tau_{\eta}],
``` |  |

which rearranges to the stated bound. If $`(\rho(\eta),\delta(\eta))`$
exist for every $`\eta>0`$, then $`\mathbb{E}[\tau_{\eta}]<\infty`$ for
all $`\eta>0`$, so $`\mathbb{E}[H_{t}]\to 0`$. ∎

## Appendix B World-Bayesian Reasoning with External Observations

We now extend the framework beyond the closed-world setting to reasoning
processes that incorporate external observations. This includes embodied
agents, tool-augmented language models, and interactive systems that
acquire information from their environment during inference ([Yao et
al., 2022](#bib.bib32); [Schick et al., 2023](#bib.bib31); [Jin et al.,
2025](#bib.bib28); [Song et al., 2025](#bib.bib33); [Kim et al.,
2025](#bib.bib27); [Luo et al., 2025](#bib.bib29)).

In contrast to the closed-world, self-Bayesian setting, we consider
*world-Bayesian reasoning*, in which the model observes additional
environmental signals that are statistically informative about the
target variable. As we show below, the availability of external
observations fundamentally changes the role of epistemic verbalization:
it is no longer the sole mechanism for escaping silent divergence, which
in turn clarifies why epistemic verbalization is so critical in the
closed-world regime studied in the main text.

#### Setup.

Let $`x`$ denote the initial input and $`Y`$ the target variable. At
each reasoning step $`t`$, the agent may take an action $`a_{t}`$ and
receive an external observation $`o_{t}\in\mathcal{O}`$, where

|     |                                         |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       o_{t}\sim P(o_{t}\mid Y,a_{t},s_{t-1}).
       ```                                      |     |

The reasoning state now evolves as

|     |                                               |     |
|-----|-----------------------------------------------|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       s_{t}:=(s_{t-1},a_{t},o_{t}),\qquad s_{0}:=x.
       ```                                            |     |

Unlike internally generated tokens, observations $`o_{t}`$ constitute
exogenous random variables that may introduce new information about
$`Y`$. Each state $`s_{t}`$ induces a predictive distribution
$`P_{\theta}(Y\mid s_{t})`$, which may now be interpreted as an
approximate Bayesian posterior updated through both self-conditioning
and external evidence.

#### Information gain from external observation.

The information gain associated with an external observation is given by

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathrm{IG}_{\mathrm{ext}}(s_{t})`$ | $`\displaystyle=H(Y\mid s_{t-1})-H(Y\mid s_{t-1},o_{t})`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle=I(Y;\;o_{t}\mid s_{t-1}).`$ |  |

This quantity is strictly non-negative and may be positive even when
procedural self-conditioning yields no additional information. In
particular, a single informative tool call or environmental observation
can resolve an ambiguity that would otherwise require extended internal
deliberation.

#### Reduced dependence on epistemic verbalization.

In the closed-world setting, the central challenge is that silent
divergence produces no overt error, leaving epistemic verbalization as
the *only* mechanism through which the model can regain traction
(Proposition [5.3](#S5.Thmtheorem3 "Proposition 5.3 (Sporadic Epistemic Verbalization Suffices for Convergence). ‣ 5.1 Epistemic Verbalization Enables Continued Information Acquisition ‣ 5 A Unified Framework: Reasoning as Strategic Information Allocation ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")).
The world-Bayesian setting relaxes this constraint. External
observations can *directly* surface errors that remain latent under
purely procedural reasoning. A tool call that returns a contradictory
result, or an environmental signal that conflicts with the model’s
current trajectory, provides an exogenous trigger for correction, one
that does not depend on the model’s ability to verbalize its own
uncertainty. In this regime, the burden of escaping silent divergence is
shared between the epistemic channel and the external observation
channel, reducing the model’s reliance on the former.

#### Residual role of epistemic verbalization.

Despite its diminished necessity, epistemic verbalization retains a
residual role in the world-Bayesian setting: it serves as an internal
monitoring signal that can trigger the *decision* to seek external
information. Recognizing that one’s current trajectory is uncertain is a
prerequisite for deciding to query a tool, request clarification, or
perform an experiment. In this sense, epistemic verbalization shifts
from being the primary mechanism of uncertainty reduction to a secondary
role as a *dispatch signal* that routes the policy toward external
actions when internal reasoning is insufficient.

#### Relationship to the main framework.

The closed-world framework arises as a special case when
$`\mathcal{O}=\emptyset`$. In this regime, all uncertainty reduction
must come from internal belief transformation, making epistemic
verbalization the sole escape route from silent divergence. The contrast
with the world-Bayesian setting highlights why epistemic verbalization
plays such a disproportionate role in the closed-world regime: these
LLMs lack external corrective signals entirely. Conversely, in
tool-augmented or interactive systems, the performance gap between
models with and without epistemic verbalization may narrow as the
external observation channel becomes richer. Empirically characterizing
this trade-off is an interesting direction for future work.

## Appendix C Limits of Internal Uncertainty in Procedural Reasoning.

A natural response to the limitations of procedural reasoning is to
leverage model uncertainty as a corrective signal. Token-level entropy,

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  |
``` math
H(A_{t}\mid s_{t-1})=-\mathbb{E}_{a^{\prime}\sim P_{\theta}(\cdot\mid s_{t-1})}\bigl[\log P_{\theta}(a^{\prime}\mid s_{t-1})\bigr].
``` |  | (4) |

has been widely studied as a proxy for reasoning uncertainty ([Yong et
al., 2025](#bib.bib17); [Yang et al., 2025b](#bib.bib25); [d’Aliberti
and Ribeiro, 2026](#bib.bib18)). While token-level entropy can serve as
a useful proxy for the model’s internal uncertainty, it captures local
confidence over the next token rather than uncertainty about the target
variable $`Y`$, and this gap limits its effectiveness as a corrective
signal.

![Refer to
caption](2603.15500v2/figure/qwen2.5_math_7b_entropy_comparison.png)

![Refer to
caption](2603.15500v2/figure/qwen3_14b_base_entropy_comparison.png)

Figure 9: Token-level entropy over reasoning steps for Qwen2.5-Math-7B
and Qwen3-14B-Base on AIME24 decreases similarly in both correct and
incorrect solutions, suggesting that entropy alone does not reliably
reflect uncertainty toward the correct answer.

Figure [9](#A3.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ Appendix C Limits of Internal Uncertainty in Procedural Reasoning. ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
illustrates a case where token-level entropy fails to distinguish
correct from incorrect reasoning: the model becomes locally more
confident at similar rates regardless of whether its trajectory is
productive, suggesting that entropy alone may not suffice as a
corrective signal.

## Appendix D Details of the Analysis

### D.1 Reasoning Collapse Analysis

This appendix details the procedure behind the reasoning-collapse
statistics in
Section [3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Procedural Reasoning and Its Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty").

#### Pipeline.

For each of the eight models analyzed in the main text, we sample
$`N{=}8`$ traces per problem across AIME24/25, AMC23, and MATH500
($`4{,}800`$ responses per model). Incorrect responses are passed to an
LLM judge (GPT-5-2025-08-07) using the prompt below, which returns a
JSON object indicating whether the trace exhibits collapse, its dominant
type, the onset sentence, and a brief justification. The collapse rate
is the fraction of incorrect responses flagged as collapsed.

#### Per-model statistics.

Table [6](#A4.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Per-model statistics. ‣ D.1 Reasoning Collapse Analysis ‣ Appendix D Details of the Analysis ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
reports aggregate results on the Qwen family. Collapse accounts for
$`54`$–$`62\%`$ of all incorrect responses ($`58.4\%`$ overall). Scaling
lowers the total error rate but leaves the share of collapse among
remaining errors roughly unchanged, indicating that larger models reduce
surface-level mistakes faster than silent divergence.

for training.

|---------------------------|---------|-------------|-------------|
| Temperature (Top-P)       |  0.0    |  0.7 (1.0)  |  0.7 (0.8)  |
| DeepSeek-R1-Distill-32B   |  50.0   |  70.0       |  80.0       |
| DeepSeek-R1-Distill-14B   |  56.67  |  56.67      |  70.0       |
| DeepSeek-R1-Distill-1.5B  |  20.0   |  30.0       |  30.0       |
| DeepSeek-Math-7B-Instruct |  3.33   |  0.0        |  0.0        |
| Qwen2.5-Math-7B           |  16.67  |  10.0       |  6.67       |
| Qwen2.5-7B                |  13.33  |  6.67       |  3.33       |
| Qwen3-1.7B-Base           |  0.0    |  0.0        |  6.67       |
| Qwen3-4B-Base             |  6.67   |  13.33      |  6.67       |

| Qwen3-14B-Base            |  16.67  |  10.0       |  13.33      |

Table 7: AIME24 pass@1 performance across various base models with
varying temperature and top-p configurations.

#### Selection of decoding hyperparameters.

We choose the decoding temperature mainly as 0.0 for calculating pass@1
and 0.7 for calculating pass@k or acc@16. However, there are some
concerns, especially for recent models that exhibit more explicit
reasoning behavior, such as DeepSeek or Qwen3, that a temperature of 0.0
may lead to performance degradation. Since we could not find detailed
guidance for the Qwen3-base model, we additionally conduct an ablation
study with varying temperatures to verify this effect when computing the
pass@1 score.

As shown in Table
[7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Training hyperparameters. ‣ Appendix E Details of the Experimental Setup ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
a temperature of 0.0 is harmful for the DeepSeek-Distill models, while
it is beneficial for the Qwen2.5 models. For the Qwen3-Base models, the
effect varies across settings. In particular, for the DeepSeek-Distill
models, setting Top-P to 0.8 provides a substantial performance gain.
Following the results in Table
[7](#A5.T7 "Table 7 ‣ Training hyperparameters. ‣ Appendix E Details of the Experimental Setup ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
we report the pass@1 performance of the base model using the larger
value between temperatures 0.0 and 0.7, while the LIMO pass@1
performance is always reported with the temperature fixed at 0.0.

## Appendix F Epistemic Verbalization Produces Information Gain

[Qian et al. (2025)](#bib.bib19) observe that, in LRM reasoning, most
steps carry little mutual information (MI) with the correct answer,
while a small number of steps exhibit sharp MI increases (“MI peaks”)
that frequently coincide with thinking tokens such as “Wait”. In this
section, we extend their analysis to examine whether epistemic
verbalization indeed induces information gain.

#### Setup.

Building on the official implementation of [Qian et al.
(2025)](#bib.bib19)
([https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks](https://github.com/ChnQ/MI-Peaks)),
we measure the statistical dependence between the hidden representation
at each token position and the ground-truth answer representation.
Specifically, for each token position $`t`$ in the model-generated
reasoning trajectory, we extract the last-layer hidden state
$`\mathbf{h}_{t}`$ and compute its mutual information with the
final-token representation of the ground-truth answer,
$`\mathbf{h}_{\text{GT}}`$, using an HSIC-based estimator ([Gretton et
al., 2007](#bib.bib26)). This enables token-level tracking of when and
how answer-relevant information emerges in the model’s internal
representations during reasoning.

#### Results.

To examine whether epistemic verbalization drives information gain, we
compare two models from the same family (Qwen3-8B-Base) on the same
problem: one that recovers the correct answer through self-correction,
and one that fails to recover. Since epistemic verbalization and
self-correction are rarely observed in Qwen3-Base, we additionally
include Qwen3-8B-SFT, fine-tuned from the same base on reasoning traces
rich in epistemic verbalization ([Ye et al., 2025](#bib.bib1)) (as shown
in
Section [6.3](#S6.SS3 "6.3 Impact of Epistemic Verbalization on Reasoning Distillation ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")),
to elicit such behavior at inference time. On AIME24 \#7, both models
initially commit to an incorrect trajectory, but only Qwen3-8B-SFT
recovers via self-correction, while Qwen3-Base remains on the incorrect
path (trajectories in
Appendix [H.2](#A8.SS2 "H.2 Comparison Between Base and LIMO Distillation ‣ Appendix H Quantitative Analysis ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")).

![Refer to caption](2603.15500v2/figure/mi/comparison_comparison.png)

Figure 10: On AIME24 \#7, both models initially fail, but only
Qwen3-8B-SFT sustains information gain through epistemic verbalization
and recovers the correct answer.

As shown in
Figure [10](#A6.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ Results. ‣ Appendix F Epistemic Verbalization Produces Information Gain ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
Qwen3-8B-Base’s MI collapses to near zero shortly after divergence,
whereas Qwen3-8B-SFT sustains elevated MI while producing evaluative
expressions such as “Wait, let me check.” A closer inspection of high-MI
regions reveals that MI tends to rise at thinking tokens, but not
always. Instead, elevated MI appears in utterances that perform
epistemic verbalization, and thinking tokens occurring *without* such
verbalization (e.g., "Hmm" in the left panel of
Figure [11](#A6.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ Results. ‣ Appendix F Epistemic Verbalization Produces Information Gain ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"))
do not trigger an MI increase.

![Refer to caption](2603.15500v2/figure/mi/mi_peak.png)

Figure 11: Token-level MI analysis: high MI aligns with evaluative
behavior, not with the thinking tokens themselves.

Aligning with our framework and the preceding discussion, these tokens
are surface manifestations of a deeper mechanism. They externalize
uncertainty, rendering the model’s epistemic state conditionable and
reusable during inference.

## Appendix G More Relationship Between Uncertainty and Epistemic Verbalization

We further investigate whether the uncertainty expressed during
reasoning truly reflects the model’s underlying uncertainty. Leveraging
the observation that more challenging problems tend to elicit greater
uncertainty, we analyze how uncertainty is verbalized in the outputs of
strong reasoning models that exhibit Aha-moment or self-reflective
behaviors.

#### DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen.

We first study DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models ranging from 1.5B to 14B
parameters, comparing their performance and response length.

Figure 12: Acc@16 (avg. score) and Len@16 (avg. response length) of
DeepSeek-Distill 1.5B–14B on math benchmarks.

As shown in
Figure [12](#A7.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen. ‣ Appendix G More Relationship Between Uncertainty and Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
more difficult problems (AIME24/25) elicit longer responses than easier
ones (AMC23/MATH500). Increasing model size is associated with higher
scores and shorter responses.

We further examined how frequently DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-{1.5B, 7B,
14B} generate epistemic tokens during solution generation. As shown in
Figure [12](#A7.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen. ‣ Appendix G More Relationship Between Uncertainty and Epistemic Verbalization ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
smaller models use these tokens more frequently: relative to the 14B
model, the 1.5B model produces 75% more occurrences of "Wait" and 235%
more of "Perhaps" in AIME24. This suggests that when reasoning models
face problems beyond their capacity, they verbalize epistemic
uncertainty more often. We also observe that epistemic tokens appear
more frequently on harder benchmarks (AIME24/25) and less frequently on
easier ones (AMC23/MATH500), indicating that these tokens indeed reflect
the uncertainty the model experiences during reasoning.

Figure 13: Token occurrence counts for DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-{1.5B,
7B, 14B} models on the AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, and MATH500 benchmarks.

#### Qwen3-Base LIMO.

Additionally, we investigated whether distilling a base model using a
teacher model that heavily incorporates epistemic verbalization leads to
increased generation of epistemic verbalizations depending on model size
and problem difficulty. We observe that, in these distilled models as
well, smaller models tend to generate more epistemic tokens as their
uncertainty about a given problem increases.

Interestingly, unlike the analysis on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen models,
where higher uncertainty substantially increased the use of the perhaps
token, these models do not show a marked increase in perhaps. Instead,
they primarily rely on the "Wait" token. As shown in Figure
[6](#S6.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 6.3 Impact of Epistemic Verbalization on Reasoning Distillation ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
this may be because the LIMO dataset contains relatively few instances
of perhaps. This suggests that patterns of uncertainty verbalization can
shift depending on the training data distribution.

Figure 14: Token occurrence counts for Qwen3-{4B, 8B, 14B}-Base models
on the AIME24, AIME25, AMC23, and MATH500 benchmarks.

## Appendix H Quantitative Analysis

### H.1 Bypass Pathways under Epistemic Token Suppression

In
Section [6.1](#S6.SS1 "6.1 Test-Time Control of Epistemic Tokens ‣ 6 Experiments ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
we suppress nine epistemic tokens (wait, hmm, perhaps, maybe, actually,
alternatively, seems, might, check) via logit bias $`-100`$ and observe
performance drops of around 10%. While suppression substantially
disrupts uncertainty expression, performance does not collapse entirely.
Analysis of the reasoning traces reveals that the models sometimes route
around the masked tokens by substituting equivalents outside the banned
vocabulary, such as hold on, no, Let me, or a paragraph break.
Table [8](#A8.T8 "Table 8 ‣ H.1 Bypass Pathways under Epistemic Token Suppression ‣ Appendix H Quantitative Analysis ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
lists the observed substitutions. In these cases, the underlying
doubt-and-verify pattern is preserved, and only its lexical surface is
rerouted.

|                         |                                            |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------|
|  Baseline surface form  |  Suppression substitute                    |
|  Wait, let me check…    |  But hold on, let me…                      |
|  Hmm,                   |  No, that’s not quite right / Hold on, no  |
|  Maybe / Perhaps        |  It’s possible that… / Suppose…            |
|  Alternatively          |  Another way to see this                   |
|  Actually               |  I realize / On closer look                |
|  Let me check           |  Let me verify                             |

Table 8: Bypass patterns observed when the epistemic tokens are
suppressed during generation.

## Appendix I Examples of Reactive and Proactive Correction

Table [9](#A10.T9 "Table 9 ‣ Appendix J Use of AI Assistants ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
lists representative examples of the two correction modes discussed in
Sections [3.3](#S3.SS3 "3.3 How Models Escape (or Fail to Escape) Collapse ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty")
and [3.4](#S3.SS4 "3.4 Proactive Correction in LRMs ‣ 3 A Self-Conditioning Framework for LLM Reasoning ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
pairing each model’s preceding computation with the verbalization that
triggers correction. Reactive corrections, observed in both LLMs and
LRMs, are triggered by an explicit failure in the preceding computation
(e.g., a violated constraint, a contradiction between derivations, or a
hallucinated runtime error). Proactive corrections, observed only in
LRMs, arise without any such surfaced error.

## Appendix J Use of AI Assistants

We used Claude and ChatGPT to polish and refine text drafted by the
authors, to create
Figure [1](#S1.F1 "Figure 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ Understanding Reasoning in LLMs through Strategic Information Allocation under Uncertainty"),
and to improve the design of plots. As described in the main text, LLMs
including GPT-5 were used as automated judges and evaluation tools as
part of the experimental pipeline. No AI assistants were used to
generate research ideas or design experiments.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Model |  Preceding computation |  Trigger verbalization |
| LLM — reactive correction only |  |  |
|  Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct |  Diagonal midpoint equation yields $`x=6`$, which explicitly violates the given constraint $`x>7`$. |  “However, we are given that $`x>7`$. Therefore, we need to re-evaluate the vertices.” |
|  Qwen2.5-7B |  Substitution gives $`y=\tfrac{5}{2z}\big|_{z=5/2}=1`$, violating the condition $`y>1`$. |  “We made an error in the interpretation of the equations.” |
|  Qwen2.5-Math-7B |  solve(...) raises TypeError: list indices must be integers or slices, not Symbol. |  “It seems there was an issue with how the solution was being accessed.” |
| LRM — reactive correction |  |  |
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B |  $`AP=\dfrac{2025-4225}{286}=\dfrac{-2200}{286}<0`$ |  “Wait, negative length? That can’t be.” |
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B |  Cayley–Menger: $`V=\frac{20\sqrt{2}}{9}`$; coordinate method: $`V=\frac{160}{3}`$ |  “That contradicts the earlier volume … So, clearly, something is wrong.” |
|  Qwen3-14B |  Numerical evaluation shows $`f(2)\approx 4.16`$, $`f(5)\approx 4.83`$, $`f(10)\approx 4.61`$: non-monotone, contradicting the earlier claim of monotonic increase. |  “Wait, so it increases up to some point and then decreases? That contradicts my previous thought.” |
| LRM — proactive correction |  |  |
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B |  Serially recalling symmedian length formulas. (each is immediately replaced by another with no computation performed.) |  “Wait, perhaps I should look for a different approach.” |
|  Qwen3-14B |  Game-tree analysis of $`n=2`$ is proceeding correctly. (no error has surfaced). |  “Wait, maybe I need to think again.” |
|  DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-32B |  Correctly identifying $`n=2`$ as a losing position for the moving player. (no contradiction present). |  “Wait, maybe I’m getting confused.” |

Table 9: Representative examples of reactive and proactive correction in
LLMs and LRMs. LLMs exhibit predominantly reactive correction, triggered
by explicit computational failures or contradiction. LRMs additionally
exhibit proactive correction, where doubt arises without any surfaced
error.
````
